question: Your pubspec says `intl: ^0.20.2` and pub refuses to take 0.21.0, yet `dio: ^5.7.0` happily moves to 5.9.0 — what is the caret doing?
answer:
The caret means "up to the next breaking version", and below 1.0.0 pub moves that boundary down a level: the minor number acts as the major.

### What each form allows
- `^5.7.0` — `>=5.7.0 <6.0.0`. Everything from the stated version up to, but not including, the next major.
- `^0.20.2` — `>=0.20.2 <0.21.0`. Major 0 means the API is still unstable, so pub treats a minor bump as breaking. That is why `intl` conflicts are so common.
- `^0.0.3` — `>=0.0.3 <0.1.0`, the same rule one level further down.
- `>=1.2.3 <2.0.0` — the long form of `^1.2.3`. Write it out only for a bound the caret cannot express, such as capping below a release you know is broken; pub has no "not equal" operator.
- `any` — every version ever published, including 0.0.1. Omitting the constraint entirely means the same thing.
- `dio: 5.9.0`, with no operator, is not a minimum. It is an exact pin.

### The traps
- A pin in a published package is a landmine: nobody can combine your package with anything else that pins the same dependency differently. Pin in an application if you must, never in a library.
- `any` does not mean "newest". It lets the solver walk backwards to an ancient version to satisfy someone else's cap, and you find out at runtime.
- The lower bound is a claim about your code: `^5.7.0` says "I use an API that appeared in 5.7.0". Setting it to whatever was newest the day you added the package excludes consumers for no reason.
- A caret does not protect you from a bad release inside its range — keeping a known-good set is the lock file's job, not the constraint's.

Rule of thumb: caret every dependency, let `pubspec.lock` hold the exact versions, and reach for the long form only to cap below something you have proven is broken.
code_example:
name: checkout_app
environment:
  sdk: ^3.9.0

dependencies:
  # ^5.7.0  ==  >=5.7.0 <6.0.0  — the usual case.
  dio: ^5.7.0

  # ^0.20.2  ==  >=0.20.2 <0.21.0
  # Below 1.0.0 the MINOR is the breaking digit, so 0.21.0 is a new
  # major and the caret will not take it. (^0.0.3 == >=0.0.3 <0.1.0.)
  intl: ^0.20.2

  # Long form: pub has no "!=", so excluding one bad release means
  # capping below it — and lifting the cap when the fix ships.
  web_socket_channel: '>=3.0.0 <3.0.3'

  # An exact pin. Legal in an app; in a published package it means
  # nobody can ever pair you with a different pin of the same dep.
  collection: 1.19.1

  # `any` accepts 0.0.1 as readily as the newest release. The solver
  # will happily go backwards to satisfy someone else's upper bound.
  crypto: any

dev_dependencies:
  # Same rules here; dev dependencies are simply not inherited.
  build_runner: ^2.4.13

# pubspec.lock is what actually pins the build:
#   dio:      version: "5.9.3"
#   intl:     version: "0.20.2"
# Constraints describe what you can accept; the lock records what you got.

question: Your app keeps `pubspec.lock` in `.gitignore`, and CI just built against a different version of a dependency than your laptop did. Who was wrong?
answer:
The app was: an application commits its lock file and a published package does not, because only one of the two is ever the root of a version solve.

### What the lock file is
`pubspec.lock` is the output of version solving — the exact version and source of every package in the graph, direct and transitive, plus a content hash for each. `pub get` reproduces that resolution instead of solving again. Delete it and pub solves from scratch, picking whatever is newest inside your constraints today, which is why two machines drifted apart.

### An application commits it
- You ship a binary built from the whole graph, not from your pubspec. Without the lock, your laptop, CI and the person who joins next month can each resolve differently.
- "Worked yesterday, broken today" becomes a diff you can read instead of an investigation.
- In CI and release builds, run `flutter pub get --enforce-lockfile`: it fails when the lock and the pubspec disagree rather than quietly rewriting the lock.

### A published package does not
- A library is never the root of anyone's resolution — the app that depends on it is, and its lock is ignored downstream. Committing one only freezes your own CI to a single combination and hides breakage against the range you advertise.
- `dart create -t package` puts `pubspec.lock` in `.gitignore` for exactly this reason.
- Test the edges of your constraints instead: one CI job on `dart pub downgrade` (the oldest versions you allow) and one on `dart pub upgrade` (the newest).

The trap is the monorepo package that is really an application. If the artifact is a binary, commit the lock no matter what the folder is called.
code_example:
# pubspec.lock — generated by pub, never hand-edited.
packages:
  dio:
    dependency: "direct main"        # you asked for it in `dependencies`
    description:
      name: dio
      sha256: "1e3a5f...c07b"        # content hash of the published tarball
      url: "https://pub.dev"
    source: hosted
    version: "5.9.3"                 # the exact version this build uses
  http_parser:
    dependency: transitive            # nobody asked for it directly
    description:
      name: http_parser
      sha256: "2a3742...9d10"
      url: "https://pub.dev"
    source: hosted
    version: "4.1.2"
  mocktail:
    dependency: "direct dev"          # from dev_dependencies
    description:
      name: mocktail
      sha256: "890df3...aa54"
      url: "https://pub.dev"
    source: hosted
    version: "1.0.4"
sdks:
  dart: ">=3.9.0 <4.0.0"
  flutter: ">=3.35.0"

# .gitignore for an APPLICATION — the lock file is NOT here:
#   build/
#   .dart_tool/
#
# .gitignore for a PUBLISHED PACKAGE (what `dart create -t package` writes):
#   build/
#   .dart_tool/
#   pubspec.lock
#
# CI, application:  flutter pub get --enforce-lockfile   # fails on drift
# CI, package:      dart pub downgrade && dart test      # oldest allowed
#                   dart pub upgrade   && dart test      # newest allowed

question: You wanted a newer `dio`, ran `flutter pub get`, and nothing moved. Which pub command is allowed to change the lock file, and how far?
answer:
`pub get` only answers questions the lock file has not already answered; moving an already-locked package is `pub upgrade`, and changing the constraint itself is `pub upgrade --major-versions`.

### The three commands
1. `flutter pub get` — reuse `pubspec.lock` wherever it still satisfies the pubspec. A newly added dependency gets solved and appended; an existing one stays exactly where it is even when a newer version fits your constraint. This is the command a build runs.
2. `flutter pub upgrade` — discard the lock's pins and re-solve for the newest versions your existing constraints allow. `flutter pub upgrade dio` limits that to one package and whatever it drags with it. `^5.7.0` reaches 5.9.3 and stops; it will never reach 6.0.0.
3. `flutter pub upgrade --major-versions` — the only one that edits `pubspec.yaml`. It rewrites constraints to admit the newest resolvable release, then solves: `^5.7.0` becomes `^6.0.0`. It does not read the changelog for you.

### The commands around them
- `flutter pub outdated` is what you run first. Current is what your lock holds, Upgradable is what `pub upgrade` would reach, Resolvable is what `--major-versions` could reach, Latest is what exists. Resolvable below Latest means something else in the graph is capping you.
- `--enforce-lockfile` makes `pub get` fail instead of changing anything — use it in CI and in release builds.
- `flutter pub upgrade --tighten` raises the lower bounds in your pubspec to the versions you actually resolved.
- `dart pub downgrade` goes the other way, to the oldest versions you allow — the fastest way to find out whether your lower bounds are honest.

The rule: `get` is deterministic, `upgrade` is a decision, `--major-versions` is a code change. Only the first belongs in an automated build.
code_example:
# Nothing moved? Ask what the lock file is holding, and what is reachable.
$ flutter pub outdated
# Package         Current  Upgradable  Resolvable  Latest
# dio             5.7.0    5.9.3       5.9.3       5.9.3
# intl            0.20.2   0.20.2      0.20.2      0.21.0  <- something caps it
# acme_analytics  1.9.4    1.9.6       2.3.0       2.3.0   <- major bump waiting

# 1) get — reuses pubspec.lock; only *new* dependencies are solved.
$ flutter pub get                      # dio stays on 5.7.0
$ flutter pub get --enforce-lockfile   # CI: fail rather than touch the lock

# 2) upgrade — re-solve inside the constraints you already wrote.
$ flutter pub upgrade dio              # 5.7.0 -> 5.9.3, still < 6.0.0
$ git diff --stat                      # pubspec.lock | 4 +--  (only the lock)

# 3) --major-versions — edits pubspec.yaml first, then solves.
$ flutter pub upgrade --major-versions acme_analytics
$ git diff pubspec.yaml
# -  acme_analytics: ^1.9.4
# +  acme_analytics: ^2.3.0
# Read the CHANGELOG before committing this. Pub did not.

# Housekeeping
$ flutter pub upgrade --tighten        # lower bounds := what you resolved
$ dart pub downgrade && flutter test   # prove those lower bounds are real
$ flutter pub get                      # restore the committed resolution

question: `flutter pub get` fails with fifteen lines of "because X depends on Y ^2.0.0..." — how do you read that wall down to the one conflict you have to fix?
answer:
Read the last sentence first: pub's solver writes a proof, and only the bottom line is about your package — everything above it exists to justify that line.

### How the message is built
Pub uses PubGrub, which records why each candidate was rejected and then prints the derivation that proved failure. Every line has the shape "because A, B", where A was established earlier.
1. Start at the bottom. The final sentence always names your root package and the two direct dependencies that cannot coexist.
2. Walk up one or two lines to the first version range you did not write yourself. That is the constraint some package imposed on the graph.
3. You now have the real pair: package P requires Q at one range, package R requires Q at an incompatible one. One of P or R has to move — Q is the messenger.

### Then collect the facts
- `flutter pub deps --style=compact` shows who pulls Q in at all, and whether it is a direct dependency or three levels down.
- `flutter pub outdated` answers "is there any solution": the Resolvable column shows the newest version reachable if constraints were relaxed. If Resolvable equals Current for the lagging package, no released version fixes this.
- The package's pub.dev versions page lists its constraints per release, which is how you find the first version of P that accepts Q 2.x.

### The fixes, best first
1. Upgrade the lagging package — often just `flutter pub upgrade --major-versions p`.
2. Downgrade the one that jumped ahead, if it is your own direct dependency and you can live a release behind.
3. Loosen your own constraint, if you were the one pinning.
4. Override against a fork, last, and with a ticket to remove it.

If the proof mentions "requires SDK version", the immovable package is the SDK, not a dependency — check the `environment` bounds before blaming anyone else.
code_example:
$ flutter pub get
Resolving dependencies...
Because every version of flutter_localizations from sdk depends on intl 0.20.2
  and acme_analytics >=2.1.0 depends on intl ^0.21.0, flutter_localizations
  from sdk is incompatible with acme_analytics >=2.1.0.
And because no versions of acme_analytics match >2.0.0 <2.1.0,
  flutter_localizations from sdk is incompatible with acme_analytics ^2.0.0.
So, because checkout_app depends on both flutter_localizations from sdk
  and acme_analytics ^2.0.0, version solving failed.

# Bottom line -> the pair is flutter_localizations vs acme_analytics.
# One line up  -> what they disagree about is `intl`.
# flutter_localizations pins intl EXACTLY, and it ships with the SDK,
# so it is the one that cannot move. acme_analytics has to.

$ flutter pub deps --style=compact | grep -n intl   # who else touches it
$ flutter pub outdated                              # is anything reachable?
# Package         Current  Upgradable  Resolvable  Latest
# acme_analytics  2.1.0    2.1.0       1.9.6       2.4.0

# Resolvable < Current: the only solution is to go back.
#   pubspec.yaml:  acme_analytics: ^1.9.6
$ flutter pub get

# Alternatives, in order: upgrade Flutter (a newer SDK pins a newer intl),
# or — last — an override, which tells the solver to stop checking:
#   dependency_overrides:
#     intl: ^0.21.0

question: One line of `dependency_overrides` turned a failing `flutter pub get` green. What did you just switch off, and what were the honest alternatives?
answer:
You told the solver to stop enforcing a constraint that a package author wrote deliberately, and to build a combination nobody has tested.

### What an override actually does
- It replaces that package everywhere in the graph — for every dependent, direct or transitive — with the version or source you name, and it silences the incompatibility rather than resolving it.
- It applies only while your package is the root of the resolution. Publish a package carrying overrides and your consumers get none of them: your CI is green and theirs is not. `dart pub publish` warns about this, and pub.dev's analysis marks it down.
- Overrides can also live in a separate `pubspec_overrides.yaml`, which is where local and machine-specific ones belong — it is also what melos and pub workspaces write for you.

### Why it bites later
- The package that declared `<0.21.0` did so because something breaks at 0.21.0. Usually it is a signature or a behaviour change, so the failure surfaces at runtime, in the path you do not test, not at compile time.
- The override is invisible in a lock file review, outlives the problem it patched, and quietly blocks the real upgrade for months.
- It hides the next conflict too: once the constraint is off, the solver stops warning you about anything involving that package.

### The honest alternatives, in order
1. Move the package that can move — upgrade the lagging one, or downgrade the one that jumped ahead. Usually a compatible release already exists.
2. Open the upstream PR that widens the constraint. It is often a one-line change a maintainer merges within days.
3. Fork it and depend on your fork by git ref, so the change is reviewable, pinned to a commit, and obviously temporary.
4. Override — with an expiry: a comment naming the upstream issue and a ticket to remove it.

An override is a patch on someone else's semver claim. If it has been in your pubspec for a year, it is a fork you never admitted to.
code_example:
# ---- Wrong: the conflict is silenced, the risk is not ----
dependencies:
  acme_analytics: ^2.1.0      # needs intl ^0.21.0
  flutter_localizations:
    sdk: flutter              # pins intl 0.20.2 exactly

dependency_overrides:
  intl: ^0.21.0               # pub get is green, and flutter_localizations
                              # now runs against an intl it was never
                              # compiled or tested against.

# ---- Better: move the package that is free to move ----
dependencies:
  acme_analytics: ^1.9.6      # last release compatible with intl 0.20.x
  flutter_localizations:
    sdk: flutter

# ---- Or: fork, so the change is pinned and reviewable ----
dependency_overrides:
  acme_analytics:
    git:
      url: https://github.com/our-org/acme_analytics.git
      ref: 4f2c9a1d           # a commit, never a branch — branches move
      # widens the intl constraint; upstream PR #412.
      # Remove when 2.2.0 ships — TICKET-2210.

# ---- Local-only overrides go in their own file, not in pubspec.yaml ----
# pubspec_overrides.yaml  (gitignored; also what melos generates)
#   dependency_overrides:
#     acme_ui:
#       path: ../acme_ui
#
# And remember: an override is ignored the moment someone else
# depends on your package. It protects your build, not theirs.

question: A reviewer says `build_runner` sitting in `dependencies` is bloating your APK. Are they right, and how do you prove what is actually in the binary?
answer:
Not directly — Dart's AOT compiler only ships code reachable from `main()`, so a package you never import adds nothing to the binary; the real cost of the wrong section is what your consumers have to resolve, and, for plugins, native code that ships regardless.

### The three buckets
- `dependencies` — resolved for you and for everyone who depends on you. Every constraint here becomes your consumers' problem too.
- `dev_dependencies` — resolved only when your package is the root: tests, `build_runner`, lints, mocks. They are not transitive, so a consumer never inherits them and they never reach the app's compile step.
- transitive — pulled in by something else. You did not choose it, you can still be broken by it, and `pubspec.lock` marks it `transitive`.

### What actually reaches the binary
- Dart code: only what is reachable. Tree shaking works per symbol, and `dart:mirrors` does not exist on mobile, so there is no reflection to defeat it.
- Assets and fonts declared by a package: shipped whether or not you use them.
- Native code from a plugin: the Android AAR or the iOS pod is linked in because the plugin is registered at build time, not because you imported it. An unused plugin costs real megabytes; an unused pure-Dart package costs close to nothing.

### How to check instead of arguing
1. `flutter build apk --release --analyze-size --target-platform=android-arm64` writes a size report; open it with DevTools' app size tool for per-package bytes.
2. `flutter pub deps --style=compact` shows who pulls in what.
3. `pubspec.lock` labels every entry `direct main`, `direct dev` or `transitive`.

The rule: anything that runs only on your machine or in CI belongs in `dev_dependencies` — not to save bytes, but so nobody downstream resolves against it.
code_example:
# Which bucket is each package in? The lock file already says.
$ grep -B3 'dependency: "direct dev"' pubspec.lock | head -20
#   dependency: "direct main"   -> yours, and inherited by your consumers
#   dependency: "direct dev"    -> dev_dependencies, never inherited
#   dependency: transitive      -> someone else asked for it

# Who dragged in a package you never chose?
$ flutter pub deps --style=compact
# checkout_app 1.4.2
# |-- dio 5.9.3
# |   |-- http_parser 4.1.2
# |   '-- web_socket_channel 3.0.3
# '-- acme_analytics 1.9.6
#     '-- http_parser 4.1.2      (one copy — pub resolves a single version)

# What is really in the binary? Measure it.
$ flutter build apk --release --analyze-size --target-platform=android-arm64
# A summary of your APK analysis can be found at:
#   build/apk-code-size-analysis_01.json
$ dart devtools --appSizeBase=build/apk-code-size-analysis_01.json

# Move the tooling where it belongs. This changes what your consumers
# resolve against — it will not change the size of the APK.
$ dart pub remove build_runner json_serializable mocktail
$ dart pub add dev:build_runner dev:json_serializable dev:mocktail
$ git diff pubspec.yaml pubspec.lock

question: A teammate points a dependency at a GitHub branch to unblock a fix. What does that cost you, and when would you accept it?
answer:
A git dependency trades version solving for a single moving pointer: it takes over that package for the entire graph, satisfies nobody else's range, and can never be published.

### The three sources
- `hosted` — the default. Immutable, versioned tarballs on pub.dev or on a private server via `hosted:`, so the solver has a range to negotiate with.
- `git` — a repo plus a `ref`, optionally a `path:` into a monorepo. The lock file records the resolved commit, so `pub get` stays reproducible; `pub upgrade` silently follows a branch ref to its new tip.
- `path` — a folder, resolved relative to the pubspec. Normal inside a monorepo where that folder is checked in beside the app; a landmine when it points outside the repo, because it then only exists on one machine.

### What it costs
- No solving. A git dependency has exactly one version. If another package needs `foo ^2.0.0` and your ref is 3.0.0-dev, pub reports a conflict it cannot negotiate away.
- Not publishable. `dart pub publish` rejects any package with a `git:` or `path:` dependency, and that applies to your internal packages too.
- Build reliability. Every developer and every CI runner now needs git access to that repo — an SSH key or token for a private one — and a force-push or a deleted branch breaks everyone at once.
- Reviewability. Nothing in your diff says what changed, because the change lives in another repository.

### When it is fine
- Pin `ref` to a commit SHA or a tag, never a branch, so the dependency stops moving.
- Use it for your own fork while an upstream PR is open, with the PR link in a comment and a ticket to remove it.
- Use it for internal packages you have not hosted yet — but once there is a second consumer, a private pub server is the better answer.

Rule of thumb: `path` for the hour you are editing two packages at once, `git` at a SHA for a fork you intend to unfork, `hosted` for everything you actually ship.
code_example:
dependencies:
  # hosted (the default) — a range the solver can negotiate
  dio: ^5.9.0

  # hosted on a private server — still versioned, still solvable
  acme_ui:
    hosted: https://pub.acme.internal
    version: ^3.2.0

  # path — a package checked in beside the app. Fine in a monorepo;
  # a landmine when it escapes it (path: ../../Users/you/dev/...).
  acme_domain:
    path: ../packages/acme_domain

  # git — WRONG. A branch ref moves under you, `pub upgrade` follows it
  # silently, and a force-push breaks every machine at once.
  #
  # acme_maps:
  #   git:
  #     url: https://github.com/acme/acme_maps.git
  #     ref: main

  # git — RIGHT. A commit, a reason, and an exit plan.
  acme_maps:
    git:
      url: https://github.com/our-org/acme_maps.git
      ref: 7c4b19e0d2            # our fork of 4.0.3; upstream PR #128
      path: packages/acme_maps   # its folder inside that repo
      # remove when upstream 4.1.0 ships — TICKET-2210

# pubspec.lock records the commit, so `pub get` stays reproducible:
#   acme_maps:
#     description:
#       path: packages/acme_maps
#       ref: 7c4b19e0d2
#       resolved-ref: "7c4b19e0d2f1a6b0c9e4..."
#       url: "https://github.com/our-org/acme_maps.git"
#     source: git
#     version: "4.0.3"

question: You bump the Flutter SDK and `pub get` dies with "requires SDK version >=2.12.0 <3.0.0" on a package nobody on the team owns. What happened, and what are your moves?
answer:
That package declared an upper bound on the Dart SDK in its own `environment:` block, pub treats that bound as hard, and every published version of it is now excluded from the solve — so the failure is about the package's metadata, not about your code.

### How the block works
- `environment: sdk: ^3.9.0` means `>=3.9.0 <4.0.0`; the caret works here too, and every package on pub.dev declares one.
- Pub filters candidate versions by that bound before solving. The rejected versions then show up in the failure proof, which is why an SDK problem reads like a dependency conflict.
- `flutter:` in the same block is a lower bound on the Flutter SDK, checked by the flutter tool rather than by the solver. In practice it has no upper bound, because the Flutter version is not part of the solve.
- Your Dart version is not chosen separately: it ships inside the Flutter SDK you selected.

### The moves, best first
1. Upgrade the package. Nine times out of ten a newer release already widened the bound; `flutter pub outdated`'s Resolvable column tells you at a glance whether any release can work.
2. Look for the maintained fork. A widely used dead package usually has one within weeks of a major Dart release, and swapping the name is cleaner than any override.
3. Override with your own fork by git ref and open the upstream PR. Widening a bound is often one line — the risk is that the package genuinely uses something Dart 3 removed.
4. Vendor it: copy the source into `packages/`, keep the licence, and own it. Honest, reviewable, and permanent for a small package.
5. Stay on the old Flutter version. Fine for a week, not for a quarter — store and plugin requirements will not wait.

The trap in the other direction is your own upper bound: shipping `sdk: '>=3.4.0 <3.9.0'` in a package you publish makes *you* the one blocking everyone's SDK bump. Publish `^3.4.0` and cap only what you have proven is broken.
code_example:
# ---- The package you do not own, as published two years ago ----
# name: legacy_charts
# environment:
#   sdk: '>=2.12.0 <3.0.0'     # hard upper bound: no candidate on Dart 3.x
#
# $ flutter pub get
# Because legacy_charts >=1.0.0 requires SDK version >=2.12.0 <3.0.0
#   and no versions of legacy_charts match >1.2.0 <2.0.0,
#   legacy_charts ^1.2.0 is forbidden.
# So, because checkout_app depends on legacy_charts ^1.2.0,
#   version solving failed.

# ---- Your app ----
name: checkout_app
environment:
  sdk: ^3.9.0            # == >=3.9.0 <4.0.0, and it comes with Flutter
  flutter: '>=3.35.0'    # lower bound only, checked by the flutter tool

dependencies:
  legacy_charts: ^1.2.0

# Move 1 — has someone already fixed it?
#   flutter pub outdated                  # look at Resolvable
#   flutter pub upgrade --major-versions legacy_charts

# Move 3 — your fork: one line changed, pinned, visible in review
dependency_overrides:
  legacy_charts:
    git:
      url: https://github.com/our-org/legacy_charts.git
      ref: 9be31c4a      # widens environment.sdk to ^3.0.0; upstream PR #77

# Publishing your own package? Never write an upper bound you have not
# verified — that is how YOUR package becomes next year's blocker:
#   sdk: '>=3.4.0 <3.9.0'   # bad: nobody can move past 3.9
#   sdk: ^3.4.0             # good: breaks only at Dart 4

question: Your team is about to publish its first package to pub.dev — what does the dry run actually check, and what can you never take back?
answer:
Publishing is permanent: pub.dev never deletes or overwrites a version, so the dry run is the last cheap check you get before the archive is public forever.

### What the dry run validates
- The pubspec: a valid name, a description pub.dev is happy with (60-180 characters scores best), a `repository` or `homepage`, and an SDK constraint that is not open-ended.
- That every dependency is hosted. A `path:` or `git:` dependency blocks the publish outright — you cannot ship something a consumer would be unable to resolve.
- The archive: which files go into it (everything not gitignored, under the size limit) and that `LICENSE`, `CHANGELOG.md` and `README.md` are there.
- It does not run your tests and it does not check that the package works for anybody else. Run `pana` locally for that — it is the same analysis that produces the pub points on the page.

### What the score is made of
- **Pub points** are mechanical: file conventions, dartdoc coverage plus an `example/`, declared platform support, a clean `dart analyze`, and constraints that allow current versions of your dependencies.
- **Likes** are human, and **downloads** replaced the old popularity percentile. None of the three says the code is good.

### What you cannot take back
A published version is immutable, and the name is claimed on the first publish and never recycled. Retracting a version from the package's admin page takes it out of version solving for new resolutions while existing lockfiles keep working — it does not unpublish anything, and every mirror already has the bytes. A secret that lands in the archive is a leaked secret. Publish from CI on a tag with pub.dev's automated publishing, so the artifact is exactly the tagged tree and no laptop is involved.
code_example:
# pubspec.yaml — the fields the dry run looks at
name: acme_result              # claimed forever on the first publish
description: A tiny Result type for Dart with pattern-matching helpers and no dependencies.
version: 0.1.0                 # pre-1.0: a breaking change bumps the minor
repository: https://github.com/acme/acme_result
issue_tracker: https://github.com/acme/acme_result/issues
topics: [functional, error-handling]

environment:
  sdk: ^3.6.0                  # an open-ended constraint fails the check

dependencies:
  meta: ^1.16.0
  # acme_internal:             # a path: or git: dependency fails the publish —
  #   path: ../acme_internal   # a consumer could never resolve it

dev_dependencies:
  test: ^1.25.0
  lints: ^5.0.0

# Never in a package you intend to publish:
# dependency_overrides:
#   meta: 1.15.0

---
# .github/workflows/publish.yml — automated publishing, no laptop involved
name: publish
on:
  push:
    tags: ['v[0-9]+.[0-9]+.[0-9]+']
jobs:
  publish:
    permissions:
      id-token: write          # the OIDC token pub.dev exchanges for publish rights
    uses: dart-lang/setup-dart/.github/workflows/publish.yml@v1

# Before any of that, locally:
#   dart pub publish --dry-run              # archive contents + pubspec validation
#   dart pub global activate pana && pana . # the score you are about to get

question: You want to add a required named parameter to a public constructor in your package — is that a patch, a minor, or a major?
answer:
Major — in Dart "breaking" means anything that can stop a consumer's code from compiling, and a new required parameter breaks every existing call site.

### Breaking, even when it looks additive
- A new required parameter, positional or named, on any public function or constructor.
- A new abstract member on a public class, because a class with no modifier can be implemented by anyone — somebody's `implements MyThing` stops compiling.
- A new value in a public enum, or a new subtype of a `sealed` class: Dart 3 switches over them are exhaustive, so consumers' `switch` expressions no longer compile.
- Narrowing a parameter type, widening a return type, renaming anything, or dropping an `export`.

### Safe
- A new optional named parameter with a default, a new top-level function, a new class, a new extension.
- A new member on a class nobody can implement or extend — which is why the class modifier you pick at 1.0.0 decides what a later addition costs you. `final class` and `interface class` keep the right to add members; a bare `class` gives it away.

### The number you actually write
- Stable: breaking is `2.0.0`, additive is `1.3.0`, a fix is `1.2.4`.
- Below 1.0.0 the caret shifts down: `^0.4.2` means `>=0.4.2 <0.5.0`, so breaking is `0.5.0` and additive is `0.4.3`.
- Shipping a breaking change as a minor is the mistake that hurts most: every consumer's caret constraint picks it up on their next `pub upgrade` and their build breaks with no change of their own.

Ask the solver's question: could a caret constraint that used to resolve now fail to compile? If yes, it is major. `dart_apitool` will diff two versions' public API when you are not sure.

question: Seven local packages, and every branch switch means running pub get in each directory — what do pub workspaces or Melos actually fix?
answer:
A workspace makes the whole repo one resolution: one `pubspec.lock`, one `.dart_tool/package_config.json`, one `pub get` at the root for every package in it.

### What a pub workspace does (Dart 3.6+)
- The root pubspec lists members under `workspace:` and each member declares `resolution: workspace`. Members still declare their own dependencies, so the boundaries stay real — the analyzer still rejects an import of a package you did not depend on.
- One solve for the whole repo means one version of every third-party package everywhere, so a mismatch between two features fails at `pub get` instead of surfacing at runtime.
- It replaces the `pubspec_overrides.yaml` files that bootstrap tools used to write to link local packages. Delete the leftovers — a stale override silently wins over the workspace.

### What Melos adds on top
- `melos exec` and named scripts to run analyze, test or codegen across packages with concurrency.
- `melos version` for conventional-commit changelogs and coordinated bumps, and ordered `melos publish` for the packages you actually ship.
- Recent versions hand linking to pub workspaces, so Melos is now release tooling rather than the linker.

### What neither fixes
- A real conflict is still a conflict. One resolution means one version, so two packages needing incompatible majors fail the entire repo.
- Native builds stay per-app; a workspace has no effect on Gradle or CocoaPods.
- Only the root's `dependency_overrides` apply, so a member cannot quietly pin something for itself.
- Every member's `environment: sdk:` has to agree with the root's — one laggard blocks the repo's SDK bump.

The mental model: a workspace is one pubspec split across directories. The single lockfile, the shared versions and the shared SDK floor all follow from that.
code_example:
# ── Before: path deps, each package resolved on its own ─────────────
# packages/auth/pubspec.yaml
#   dependencies:
#     acme_core: { path: ../core }
# packages/auth/pubspec_overrides.yaml   <- generated, gitignored, easy to
#                                           leave behind and hard to notice

# ── After: one workspace ────────────────────────────────────────────
# pubspec.yaml (repo root) — has no lib/, is never published
name: acme_workspace
publish_to: none
environment:
  sdk: ^3.6.0
workspace:
  - app
  - packages/core
  - packages/auth
  - packages/billing

dev_dependencies:
  melos: ^6.3.0

# Only the ROOT may override; a member's dependency_overrides is ignored
dependency_overrides:
  stale_plugin: ^2.1.0        # github.com/acme/app/issues/812, drop after 2.2

melos:
  scripts:
    analyze: { run: dart analyze, exec: { concurrency: 4 } }
    test:    { run: flutter test, exec: { concurrency: 2, failFast: true } }

---
# packages/auth/pubspec.yaml
name: acme_auth
resolution: workspace         # opts this package into the root's single solve
environment:
  sdk: ^3.6.0                 # must be compatible with every other member
dependencies:
  flutter: { sdk: flutter }
  acme_core: ^1.0.0           # a declared dependency, not a path — boundary kept

# One command for the whole repo, one lockfile at the root:
#   flutter pub get
#   git status    # -> only ./pubspec.lock ever changes

question: A transitive dependency you never chose ships a broken patch on Friday and your build starts failing — what do you do first?
answer:
First establish whether it can even reach you: with `pubspec.lock` committed and CI running `pub get --enforce-lockfile`, a bad publish upstream changes nothing until somebody deliberately upgrades.

### Find the real culprit
1. `dart pub deps --style=compact` shows who pulls the package in — usually one direct dependency you do own.
2. `git diff pubspec.lock` on the failing branch shows exactly which versions moved. If the lockfile is unchanged and CI still broke, something resolved fresh, and that is the bug to fix first.
3. Read the package's changelog and open issues before assuming the fault is yours.

### The options, cheapest first
- **Stop the drift.** Everyone back on the committed lockfile, `--enforce-lockfile` in CI. This buys you the weekend and costs nothing.
- **Constrain it yourself.** Add the transitive package to your own `dependencies:` with a range that excludes the bad version. A direct dependency is the supported way to bound a transitive one, and the solver tells you immediately if that range is impossible.
- **Report it upstream** and ask the maintainer to retract the version. A retracted version stops being chosen by every new resolution, which fixes it for everyone rather than only for you.
- **`dependency_overrides`**, last. It works, it is ignored for anyone who depends on you, and it keeps applying long after upstream ships the fix — so it needs a comment with an issue link and a date.

The trap is pinning to an exact version. `broken_json: 1.4.2` looks decisive and becomes the next conflict the moment another package needs `^1.5.0`; `broken_json: '>=1.4.0 <1.4.3'` says the same thing without cornering the solver.
code_example:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# 1) Who pulls it in, and what actually moved?
dart pub deps --style=compact | grep -B3 broken_json
git diff HEAD~1 -- pubspec.lock | grep -B2 broken_json

# 2) Prove CI ships the lockfile: this fails instead of quietly re-resolving
flutter pub get --enforce-lockfile

# 3) Reproduce the way a fresh clone sees it, then put the lockfile back
rm -rf .dart_tool pubspec.lock && flutter pub get && flutter test
git checkout -- pubspec.lock

# 4) Bound it yourself — a direct dependency is how you constrain a transitive
dart pub add "broken_json:>=1.4.0 <1.4.3"     # NOT broken_json:1.4.2
#   dependencies:
#     broken_json: '>=1.4.0 <1.4.3'   # 1.4.3 throws on an empty list
#                                     # github.com/vendor/broken_json/issues/91

# 5) Or step back one version, verify, and commit the lockfile deliberately
dart pub downgrade broken_json
flutter test && git add pubspec.lock pubspec.yaml

# Last resort — dated, linked, and deleted the day upstream ships:
#   dependency_overrides:
#     broken_json: 1.4.2   # TODO(#812) remove after 1.4.4 — added 2026-03-13

question: Why does one camera plugin turn into five packages on pub.dev, and which of them does your app actually depend on?
answer:
A federated plugin splits the Dart-facing API from each platform's implementation so a platform can be added by somebody who does not own the plugin — and your app depends only on the app-facing package.

### The packages
- The **app-facing** package (`path_provider`) — the API you import. It holds almost no logic.
- The **platform interface** (`path_provider_platform_interface`) — an abstract class plus a static `instance` that everything talks through.
- One **platform implementation** each (`path_provider_android`, `path_provider_foundation`, `path_provider_linux`, `path_provider_windows`), all implementing that interface.

### How an implementation gets picked up
1. The app-facing package **endorses** it: it depends on the implementation and names it under `flutter: plugin: platforms: <platform>: default_package:`.
2. So `pub get` pulls the implementation into your app, and the tool's generated registrant calls its `registerWith()`, which sets `PathProviderPlatform.instance = PathProviderAndroid()`.
3. An unendorsed implementation — a third party's Windows build, say — goes into your app's own `dependencies:` instead, and registers the same way.

### The details that bite
- The interface extends `PlatformInterface` and every implementation must `extends` it and pass the token, checked by `PlatformInterface.verify` (the older `verifyToken` is deprecated). `implements` is deliberately rejected so the interface can add a method with a default body without breaking every implementation — the whole point of the split.
- Your version-solve failure is usually two implementations disagreeing about the platform interface's version, not about the plugin.
- A Dart-only implementation sets `dartPluginClass` with `pluginClass: none`; there is no native side to register.

Mental model: the platform interface is a service locator, and endorsement is one `default_package:` line of YAML.
code_example:
# ── 1. app-facing package: the API plus the endorsements ────────────
# bar_scanner/pubspec.yaml
name: bar_scanner
dependencies:
  flutter: { sdk: flutter }
  bar_scanner_platform_interface: ^2.0.0
  bar_scanner_android: ^2.1.0      # endorsed -> lands in every consumer
  bar_scanner_ios: ^2.1.0
flutter:
  plugin:
    platforms:
      android:
        default_package: bar_scanner_android
      ios:
        default_package: bar_scanner_ios
      # no `web:` entry -> the web implementation is unendorsed

# ── 2. one platform implementation ──────────────────────────────────
# bar_scanner_android/pubspec.yaml
name: bar_scanner_android
dependencies:
  flutter: { sdk: flutter }
  bar_scanner_platform_interface: ^2.0.0
flutter:
  plugin:
    implements: bar_scanner        # this line makes it an implementation
    platforms:
      android:
        package: com.acme.bar_scanner
        pluginClass: BarScannerPlugin   # Dart-only instead:
        # dartPluginClass: BarScannerAndroid
        # pluginClass: none

# ── 3. your app ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# app/pubspec.yaml
dependencies:
  bar_scanner: ^2.1.0              # android + ios arrive with it
  bar_scanner_web: ^0.3.0          # unendorsed: you add this one yourself

# Do NOT list bar_scanner_android here. You would be pinning a version the
# app-facing package never agreed to, and the solve breaks on its next release.

question: Your team upgrades dependencies twice a year and each round costs two days of firefighting — how do you make upgrades boring?
answer:
Turn one big bang into a stream of small reviewable bumps, and be explicit about the few things you pin on purpose and never float.

### Read `pub outdated` properly first
`flutter pub outdated` prints four columns and each means something different. **Current** is your lockfile. **Upgradable** is what `pub upgrade` can reach without touching pubspec.yaml. **Resolvable** is what you could reach by changing constraints. **Latest** is what exists. A package whose Upgradable equals Current but whose Resolvable is higher is held back by *your* constraint; one whose Resolvable is below Latest is held back by *another package's* constraint, and the fix lives upstream.

### Automate the boring half
- Dependabot has a `pub` ecosystem and Renovate has a pub manager; either opens PRs on a schedule.
- Group them — all dev dependencies in one PR, all patch bumps in another — or you get twenty PRs a week and review none of them.
- Automerge is only safe when the PR runs analyze, tests and a build, and CI uses `pub get --enforce-lockfile` so what merges is what was tested.
- `dart pub upgrade --tighten` raises lower bounds to the versions you actually resolved, so your constraints stop claiming support you never tested.

### What you pin on purpose
- The Flutter/Dart SDK: pinned in one place and read by CI, the Docker image and every developer. It is not a pub dependency, so none of the bots above will manage it.
- Code generators whose output is committed — `build_runner`, `freezed`, `json_serializable`. Bump them in a PR that regenerates in the same commit.
- Anything with native code your CI cannot actually exercise.
- Any workaround pin, with a comment, an issue link and a date.

`pub upgrade --major-versions` rewrites your constraints for you. That is the PR a human reads line by line — never the one you automerge.
code_example:
# .github/dependabot.yml
version: 2
updates:
  - package-ecosystem: pub
    directory: /
    schedule: { interval: weekly, day: monday }
    open-pull-requests-limit: 5
    groups:
      dev-dependencies:              # one PR for the whole tooling tier
        dependency-type: development
      patch-bumps:
        update-types: [patch]
    ignore:
      - dependency-name: build_runner          # generated output is committed:
        update-types:                          # bump by hand and regenerate
          - version-update:semver-minor        # in the same commit
          - version-update:semver-major
      - dependency-name: acme_native_sdk       # CI cannot exercise the native half

---
# .github/workflows/deps.yml — what makes automerge safe
jobs:
  verify:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: subosito/flutter-action@v2
        with:
          flutter-version-file: pubspec.yaml   # the SDK is pinned in ONE place
      - run: flutter pub get --enforce-lockfile  # merge exactly what was tested
      - run: flutter analyze --fatal-infos
      - run: flutter test

# Monthly, by a human, never automerged:
#   flutter pub outdated --show-all
#   dart pub upgrade --tighten          # constraints match what you tested
#   dart pub upgrade --major-versions   # rewrites pubspec.yaml — read the diff

question: Two packages in your monorepo need incompatible major versions of the same dependency — what does pub do, and how do you get out?
answer:
Pub resolves one version of every package for the whole resolution, so there is no "both" — the solve fails, and every real fix ends with one of the two constraints moving.

### Why there is no both
Dart has one `package_config.json` per resolution and one copy of each library in the program. Two versions of `analytics` would mean two distinct `analytics.Event` types that are not assignable to each other, so pub refuses rather than produce that. This is not npm's nested `node_modules` and not Gradle quietly picking the newest: a conflict is a hard failure at `pub get`. In a workspace it is repo-wide — one lockfile, one version for every member.

### Getting out, in order
1. Read the solver's `because` chain to the end. It names the two constraints; decide whether you own either of them.
2. Bump the laggard. Nine times out of ten one side is simply old and a newer release already widened its constraint.
3. If the laggard is third-party and unmaintained, send a PR that only widens the constraint — the most mergeable PR in open source — and depend on your fork by `git:` with a pinned `ref:` while you wait.
4. Isolate. If the two consumers never exchange the dependency's types, put your own interface between them and it, so only one package in the repo depends on it at all.
5. `dependency_overrides` in the workspace root, forcing one version and accepting that one consumer now runs against a major it never declared. Test that consumer specifically.

An override in a member's pubspec does nothing — in a workspace only the root's overrides apply. And two versions genuinely coexist only across a process boundary: a separate app outside the workspace, never two packages in one binary.

The framing that helps: a version conflict is a scheduling problem, not a technical one. Somebody has to do a bump; the only questions are who and when.
code_example:
# What the failure actually looks like
$ flutter pub get
# Because acme_billing depends on analytics ^3.0.0 and acme_auth depends on
# analytics ^2.4.0, version solving failed.

# 1) Read the chain to the end, then see who really pulls it in
dart pub deps --style=compact | grep -B3 analytics
dart pub deps --json | jq '.packages[] | select(.name == "analytics")'

# 2) Is the laggard already fixed upstream? Resolvable vs Latest answers it
dart pub outdated --show-all --transitive

# 3) Move the constraint you own
#    packages/auth/pubspec.yaml
#      dependencies:
#        analytics: ^3.0.0          # was ^2.4.0 — migration in #914

# 4) Third-party laggard: fork, widen, pin the commit
#    dependencies:
#      stale_sdk:
#        git:
#          url: https://github.com/acme/stale_sdk.git
#          ref: 3f9c1ab             # a commit; `ref: main` is not reproducible
#      # upstream PR: github.com/vendor/stale_sdk/pull/44

# 5) Last resort — ROOT pubspec only; a member's overrides are ignored
#    dependency_overrides:
#      analytics: ^3.0.0            # acme_auth now runs on an undeclared major
flutter pub get && melos exec -- flutter test

question: A package at the centre of your app has not shipped in two years and now blocks a Dart SDK bump — fork, vendor, or replace?
answer:
Decide by how much of the package you actually use and how much native code it carries, then keep the change reviewable by not touching your own import sites in the same PR.

### Read the situation first
Check whether the author marked it discontinued on pub.dev — that page also carries a suggested replacement, which is the maintainer telling you where to go. Then count your call sites with `grep -r "package:foo/"` and look at whether it ships `android/` or `ios/` directories. Twelve call sites of pure Dart is a completely different problem from a plugin with a Kotlin half.

### The options and what each costs
- **Pin and wait.** Pin the SDK and buy a few weeks. It eventually blocks every other upgrade, so give it an expiry date, not an opinion.
- **Fork and publish** under your own publisher. You now own CI, the changelog and the next security fix — worth it when several apps in the company need the same fix.
- **Fork and depend by `git:` with a pinned `ref:`.** Fastest, and fine for an application. A package you publish may not have a git dependency at all, so it is a dead end for anything going to pub.dev.
- **Vendor it** into `packages/foo/` and delete what you do not use. Best when you use 10% of it; you keep the LICENSE and its attribution, and you inherit the patches nobody will now send you.
- **Replace it.** The only option that shrinks total code, and the only one that is a real project.

### Keeping it reviewable
1. Write characterization tests against today's behaviour before you change anything.
2. If forty files import it, the first PR wraps it behind your own interface and changes nothing else; the second swaps the implementation and touches one file.
3. Record the decision in the pubspec: the pinned commit, the upstream issue, the date.

Forks are cheap to create and expensive to own. The deciding question is not "can I fix it" but "who merges the next fix".
code_example:
# ── The decision, written where the next person will find it ────────
# pubspec.yaml
dependencies:

  # 1) Pin and wait — an expiry date, not an opinion
  legacy_charts: 2.3.1           # blocks the Dart 3.7 bump; revisit 2026-06-01 (#1204)

  # 2) Fork, depended on by commit. Fine for an app; a package published to
  #    pub.dev may not carry a git dependency at all.
  pdf_render:
    git:
      url: https://github.com/acme/pdf_render.git
      ref: 8a41c02               # a commit — `ref: main` is not reproducible
    # fork of vendor/pdf_render 1.9.2 with the SDK constraint widened
    # upstream PR: github.com/vendor/pdf_render/pull/88 (open since 2024-11)

  # 3) Vendored: the 300 lines we used out of 4k, LICENSE and NOTICE kept
  acme_barcode:
    path: packages/acme_barcode

  # 4) Replaced — the old name survives only as archaeology
  # tiny_uuid: ^1.0.0            -> replaced by package:uuid (#1211)
  uuid: ^4.5.0

# ── Step one of any swap: wrap, do not replace ──────────────────────
# lib/src/charts/chart_series.dart exposes your own types only, so the 40
# files that imported package:legacy_charts/ now import that. The second PR
# changes that one file and nothing else.

# ── CI keeps the fork honest ────────────────────────────────────────
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
#   - run: flutter pub get --enforce-lockfile  # a git dep still gets locked
#   - run: dart run tool/check_forks.dart      # fails a `git:` dep whose ref
#                                              # is a branch instead of a commit
